role.q: How do you start a new project?
role.why: The first question of most project manager interviews: they want to hear framing before planning.
role.model: I start by framing it with the sponsor: why the project exists, the expected benefits, what is in and out of scope, the deadline, the budget and the constraints. I write that in a short project charter and get it signed off. Then I identify the stakeholders and how much each one is involved, I meet the team, and I break the work down into deliverables and tasks to build a first plan with milestones, estimates from the people who will do the work, a budget and a first list of risks. I set up the governance: a weekly team meeting, a status report and a steering committee. Only then do we start the work.

role.q: Your project is going to be late. What do you do?
role.why: Every project slips; they want to see you act early and tell the truth.
role.model: First I measure how late and why, with the people doing the work, and I check the critical path: is the delay on it? Then I look at the options: re-sequence tasks, add people where it really helps, reduce or split the scope, or move the date. I estimate each option’s cost and risk. I go to the sponsor early, before the date is missed, with the facts and a recommendation, not just a problem; the sponsor decides. Afterwards I update the plan, tell everyone affected, and note what caused the delay so it does not happen again.

role.q: How do you manage risks on a project?
role.why: Risk management is in every PM job description and every certification.
role.model: I keep a risk register from the start: each risk with its probability, impact, owner and response, which can be to avoid, reduce, transfer or accept it. I review it every week with the team and add new risks as they appear. The highest risks get a concrete action with a date, and some get a contingency plan. I also keep part of the budget or the schedule as a reserve for unknowns. I report the top three risks at each steering committee so decisions are made in time, and I close a risk when it can no longer happen.

role.q: Agile or waterfall: which do you prefer?
role.why: They want judgement, not a slogan: the method depends on the project.
role.model: It depends on how well the requirements are known and how costly change is. When the scope is stable and the result must be built in a fixed order, for example moving offices or a regulatory change with a set date, a plan-driven approach with phases works well. When users’ needs are uncertain, as in most software products, agile delivery in short iterations lets us learn and change direction cheaply. Many projects I would run as hybrid: a milestone plan and a budget for the sponsor, with Scrum or Kanban teams delivering inside it, and the plan updated from what the teams actually deliver.

role.q: Tell me about a conflict in a team and how you handled it.
role.why: A behavioural question: they want a STAR story that shows you listen and decide.
role.model: Situation: on a student project, two team members disagreed on the technical approach and the work stopped for three days. Task: as the project lead I had to unblock the team without taking sides blindly. Action: I met each of them separately to understand their reasons, then brought them together with the criteria that mattered for the project, the deadline and the client’s needs, and asked each to explain how their option met them. We chose one option and planned a small test for the risk the other had raised. Result: work restarted the same day and we delivered on time. What I learned: most conflicts are about different priorities, so make the priorities explicit.

role.q: How do you report on the status of a project?
role.why: Communication is most of the job: they want to know what you report, to whom, and how honestly.
role.model: I adapt the report to the audience. For the steering committee, a one-page status: overall status in green, amber or red with the reason, milestones achieved and next ones, budget used against plan, the top risks and issues, and the decisions I need from them. For the team, the detailed plan and actions. I keep the status honest: an amber reported early is better than a red discovered late. I send it at a fixed rhythm, for example every Friday, and I use a dashboard in Power BI or Excel so the numbers come from the plan and not from my memory.

role.q: What is the critical path and why does it matter?
role.why: A technical question that checks you can actually build and read a plan.
role.model: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks from the start to the end of the project; it gives the shortest possible duration. Tasks on it have no float: if one of them is late by a day, the project ends a day late, unless something changes. Tasks off the critical path have some margin. It matters because it tells me where to focus: I watch critical tasks closely, put the best resources on them and look there first when I need to shorten the project. The critical path can change as the project moves, so I recalculate it when the plan is updated.

role.q: How do you manage a project budget?
role.why: Budget control is a core part of the role, and recruiters want concrete practice.
role.model: I build the budget from the plan: people’s time, licences, suppliers and a contingency reserve for the main risks, and I get it approved. During the project I track actual costs and commitments against the plan every month, and I forecast the cost at completion, not only what has been spent. If the forecast goes over, I find the cause, look at the options (scope, timing, supplier terms) and go to the sponsor with a recommendation before the money runs out. Changes in scope go through a change request with their cost, so the budget and the scope stay aligned.
